sentences.text: The name Hainosaurus means 'lizard from the Haine', referring to the river near its discovery site.
Hainosaurus is considered one of the largest mosasaurs, although its estimated size has been revised multiple times.
The skeleton includes 53 vertebrae extending from the neck to the tail region where chevrons are found, a count significantly higher than the 35 vertebrae seen in the related genus Tylosaurus.
Consequently, the tail of Hainosaurus is shorter than that of Tylosaurus because it possesses fewer vertebrae that bear these chevron structures.
The estimated length of Hainosaurus has varied significantly, ranging from an initial estimate of 17 meters to a recent estimate of 12.2 meters.
The genus Hainosaurus was described by Louis Dollo in 1885 based on a skeleton found in a phosphate quarry near Mesvin, Belgium.
The species name bernardi honors Leopold Bernard, the industrialist who funded the excavation of the holotype skeleton — the specimen the species is based on.
The holotype skeleton of Hainosaurus bernardi is currently housed at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences with catalog number IRSNB R23.
A second species, Hainosaurus pembinensis, was described in 1988 by Elizabeth Nicholls from fossils found in Manitoba, Canada.
There are 16 recorded fossil occurrences of Hainosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
While the documentary suggested they traveled in large family groups, most Tylosaurinae and mosasaurs likely lived alone and only gathered during mating or when mothers gave birth.
Hainosaurus belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
Hainosaurus is classified within the mosasaur subfamily Tylosaurinae and is closely related to the genus Tylosaurus.
The genus authority for Hainosaurus is attributed to Dollo, 1885.
Fossils of Hainosaurus date from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Hainosaurus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
In 2010, researchers Bullard and Caldwell argued that the specimen previously identified as Hainosaurus pembinensis actually belonged to the genus Tylosaurus due to a revised vertebral count.
Some scientists debate the synonymy of Hainosaurus with Tylosaurus, citing unexplored differences in tooth morphology, specifically an advanced cutting-based dentition.
